etymology: The Authorized Version’s older spelling of veils, from Old French veile, from the Latin velum, “a covering, a curtain, a sail”; hence a cloth worn over the head or face. The KJV keeps both the archaic spelling and, in Isaiah, the plural form.
biblical_def: Vails are the head-coverings and face-cloths of women — the plural naming not the great curtain of the temple but the wardrobe of the daughters of Zion. Isaiah numbers them last in a long inventory of finery the LORD will strip away in the day of His visiting: “The glasses, and the fine linen, and the hoods, and the vails” (Isa 3:23). Even a modest thing becomes a vanity when it is worn for the eye of man rather than the fear of God. Yet Scripture’s first use of the vail is honourable. When Rebekah lifted her eyes and saw Isaac walking in the field, “she took a vail, and covered herself” (Gen 24:65) — the bride veiling herself before her husband, modesty and reverence in a single gesture, the creational order worn upon the head. Tamar turned the covering to deceit, putting off her widow’s garments and covering herself with a vail to sit by the way (Gen 38:14), for what God gives for modesty the fallen heart will bend to seduction. And in the Song the watchmen tore the covering from the bride: “the keepers of the walls took away my veil from me” (Son 5:7) — a violence against a woman which Scripture records with grief. The vail therefore preaches what the age will not hear: that a woman’s covering is neither bondage nor ornament but honour, and that God orders even the cloth upon the head (1Co 11:3-10).
webster_summary: The KJV spelling of veils; the cloths worn by women over head or face, named among the finery of Zion’s daughters.
webster_full: VAIL, a cloth worn over the head or face; a covering; the older spelling of veil.
From the Latin velum, “a covering, a curtain.”
In the plural, the head-coverings among Zion’s finery, swept away in judgment (Isa 3:23).
Rebekah took a vail and covered herself before Isaac (Gen 24:65).
Distinct from the great vail of the temple, rent at the death of Christ.
scriptures: Isa 3:23
The glasses, and the fine linen, and the hoods, and the vails.
For she had said unto the servant, What man is this that walketh in the field to meet us? And the servant had said, It is my master: therefore she took a vail, and covered herself.

And she put her widow's garments off from her, and covered her with a vail, and wrapped herself, and sat in an open place, which is by the way to Timnath; for she saw that Shelah was grown, and she was not given unto him to wife.
Son 5:7
The watchmen that went about the city found me, they smote me, they wounded me; the keepers of the walls took away my veil from me.
corruption_summary: A live corruption: the age counts the covering an insult and modesty a bondage, where Scripture makes it honour and the creational order worn upon the head.
corruption_paragraphs: Here is a real corruption, and it is not subtle. The age has taught that a woman’s covering is a badge of subjection imposed by men, and that to uncover is to be free; and so it reads Rebekah’s vail as a chain and Paul’s ordering of the head as an embarrassment the church should outgrow. Scripture says otherwise. The LORD made man and woman, and He ordered them: the head of the woman is the man, and the head of Christ is God (1Co 11:3). The covering is not contempt for the woman but honour set upon her — a glory, as her long hair is given her for a covering. To strip the vail in the name of liberty is not to raise the woman but to unmake the order in which God set her, and no daughter of Eve was ever made freer by despising what her Maker appointed.

Yet Isaiah’s rebuke cuts the other way, and the church must hear it too. The vails he names are not the modest coverings of believing women but the finery of the haughty daughters of Zion, worn with stretched-forth necks and wanton eyes and tinkling feet. A covering worn to be seen is no covering at all; the heart that dresses for the eye of man has already uncovered itself before God. So the LORD threatens to take away the glasses and the fine linen and the hoods and the vails together, for He will have the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which in His sight is of great price. Modesty is not a length of cloth but a fear of God, and where that fear is absent the vail is only one vanity more.
roots_summary: The word means a cloth covering worn over the head or face; the KJV spelling of veils.

Numbered among the finery stripped from Zion’s daughters (Isa 3:23).

usage: Rebekah took a vail and covered herself: the bride veiled in modesty before her husband.

etymology: From the Old French couvrechief, “cover-head,” from couvrir (“to cover”) and chief (“head”); hence a cloth for the head. In Ezekiel it names the long veils the false prophetesses made and set upon the heads of their clients.
biblical_def: A kerchief is a cover for the head — the word is literally “cover-chief,” a cloth laid over the crown. In all Scripture it appears only in one dark chapter, and there it is an instrument of soul-hunting. Ezekiel is sent against the daughters of his people who prophesy out of their own heart: they sew pillows to all armholes and make kerchiefs upon the head of every stature to hunt souls (Eze 13:18). Here is a trade in charms. The women fitted their wares to every customer — a kerchief for every stature, cut to the measure of the one who paid — and with soft cushions and covered heads they promised life to those the LORD had not quickened and death to those He had not condemned. The LORD’s answer is a tearing: “Your kerchiefs also will I tear, and deliver my people out of your hand, and they shall be no more in your hand to be hunted; and ye shall know that I am the LORD” (Eze 13:21). He is against their pillows and will let the hunted souls go free (Eze 13:20), until they see no more vanity nor divine divinations (Eze 13:23). The kerchief therefore stands for every religious article sold to the anxious — the covering that comforts the head while the soul goes unwarned. God tears such coverings off, and the tearing is mercy.
webster_summary: A cloth for covering the head; in Ezekiel, the veils the false prophetesses made to hunt souls, which the LORD promised to tear.
webster_full: KERCHIEF, a cloth to cover the head; literally “cover-chief.”
From Old French couvrechief, from couvrir, “to cover,” and chief, “head.”
It occurs in Scripture only of the false prophetesses of Ezekiel 13.
Made upon the head of every stature, cut to the measure of the buyer, to hunt souls.
The LORD promised to tear the kerchiefs and set the hunted souls free (Eze 13:21).
scriptures: Your kerchiefs also will I tear, and deliver my people out of your hand, and they shall be no more in your hand to be hunted; and ye shall know that I am the LORD.

Wherefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I am against your pillows, wherewith ye there hunt the souls to make them fly, and I will tear them from your arms, and will let the souls go, even the souls that ye hunt to make them fly.
Therefore ye shall see no more vanity, nor divine divinations: for I will deliver my people out of your hand: and ye shall know that I am the LORD.
Thus saith the LORD of hosts, Hearken not unto the words of the prophets that prophesy unto you: they make you vain: they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD.
corruption_summary: A live corruption: the trade Ezekiel condemned is still open, and the modern market in prophetic words and holy trinkets hunts souls with kerchiefs of its own.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption named here is not ancient but present. Ezekiel’s women prophesied out of their own heart and sold the comfort of it, fitting a kerchief to the head of every stature — and the same shop is open today. The self-appointed prophet who sells a word from the Lord, the anointed cloth mailed to the giver, the point-of-contact trinket, the prophetic conference where a vision of a man’s own heart is priced and delivered: these are kerchiefs. The dictionary is cessationist with the Reformed churches: the canon is closed, and no man now speaks new revelation. Deuteronomy sentences the prophet who presumes to speak a word the LORD has not commanded, and Jeremiah bids the people hearken not to prophets who make them vain. To take money for a word God never spoke is to hunt the souls of His people.

Mark what the kerchief actually does: it covers the head and leaves the soul unwarned. That is the whole art of the false prophetess — to lay something soft where God would lay conviction, to promise life to those He has not quickened and to slay the souls that should live. The faithful minister has no wares to sell and no covering to offer but Christ; he preaches the Word, and the Word wounds before it heals. And the LORD’s judgment upon the whole trade is a mercy to the hunted: “Your kerchiefs also will I tear, and deliver my people out of your hand.” He strips the covering to save the soul under it, and the delivered people know at last that He is the LORD.
roots_summary: The word means a cloth for covering the head — literally a “cover-chief.”
roots_lines: Kerchief — Old French couvrechief, “cover-head.”
From couvrir, “to cover,” and chief, “head.”
It denotes a cloth laid over the crown of the head.
In Ezekiel it names the charm-veils of the false prophetesses.
The LORD tears the kerchief to free the hunted soul (Eze 13:21).
usage: They made kerchiefs upon the head of every stature — a charm cut to the measure of the buyer.
Your kerchiefs also will I tear: God strips the covering to deliver the soul beneath it.
Every prophetic word sold for money is a kerchief, and the trade hunts souls still.

etymology: From the Old English hār, “grey, venerable, old,” whence also hoar (as in hoar-frost); hence white or grey with age. The hoary head is the head grown white with years.
biblical_def: Hoary means white or grey with age — the same word that names the hoar-frost lying white upon the ground names the head grown white with years. Scripture never treats that whiteness as a defect. The law commands a posture toward it: “Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God: I am the LORD” (Lev 19:32). Mark the yoking of the two commands. To rise when age enters the room and to fear God are set in one breath, for the honour paid to grey hairs is honour paid to the God who gave them; a man who will not stand for the aged has already sat down before his Maker. Solomon adds the crown: “The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness” (Pro 16:31). The condition is not idle. Grey hairs are a crown, but a crown of glory only where the years have been spent in the way of righteousness; a long life of sin whitens the head without adorning it, and David could charge Solomon to bring Shimei’s hoar head down to the grave with blood (1Ki 2:9). So the word holds both an honour and a warning: the beauty of old men is the gray head (Pro 20:29), and the fifth commandment reaches from a child’s father to every white head in Israel.
webster_summary: White or grey with age; the hoary head is the head grown white with years, a crown of glory in the way of righteousness.
webster_full: HOARY, white or whitish; grey with age; the same word as hoar, of frost.
From the Saxon hār, “grey, venerable, old.”
The hoary head is the head made white by many years.
Israel was commanded to rise up before it and fear God (Lev 19:32).
It is a crown of glory, if found in the way of righteousness (Pro 16:31).
scriptures: Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God: I am the LORD.
The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness.
The glory of young men is their strength: and the beauty of old men is the gray head.
Do therefore according to thy wisdom, and let not his hoar head go down to the grave in peace.
corruption_summary: A live corruption: an age that worships youth has emptied the fifth commandment of the honour Scripture commands toward every hoary head.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption here is a settled contempt, and it is everywhere. The age worships youth, prices the old out of usefulness, warehouses them where they will not be seen, and jokes at the white head as though decay were a failure of will. Its whole vocabulary is against the hoary head: the new is progress, the old is out of date, and a man is finished when his strength goes. Scripture commands the opposite posture, and commands it as an act of worship: “Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God.” The honour and the fear are one command. He who despises the grey head despises the God who whitened it, and the fifth commandment is not satisfied by tenderness to one’s own parents while every other aged saint is passed by.

But the honour is not flattery, and Solomon guards it with a condition. The hoary head is a crown of glory — if it be found in the way of righteousness. Years alone confer nothing; a man may grow old in folly and carry a white crown upon an empty head, and David could bid Solomon bring Shimei’s hoar head down to the grave with blood. So the word speaks to both ends of life. To the young it says, rise up, uncover, and learn; the beauty of old men is the gray head, and the strength you glory in will be gone in forty years. To the old it says, the crown is given to a life spent in the way of righteousness — therefore finish well, that the whiteness upon your head may be a glory and not a reproach.
roots_summary: The word means white or grey with age — the head made white by many years.
roots_lines: Hoary — Old English hār, “grey, venerable, old.”

It describes the head whitened by age, and the man who bears it.
Israel must rise before the hoary head and fear God (Lev 19:32).
It is a crown of glory only in the way of righteousness (Pro 16:31).
usage: Rise up before the hoary head and fear thy God: the honour and the fear are one command.
The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness — not otherwise.
The glory of young men is their strength; the beauty of old men is the gray head.

etymology: From the Old French greve, “shin, the front of the leg”; hence the armour worn upon the shin, plates of brass or leather guarding the leg from knee to ankle. A KJV word occurring but once.
biblical_def: Greaves are shin-armour — plates strapped over the leg from knee to ankle, guarding the part a footman most easily loses. The word occurs but once in Scripture, and it is fastened to a giant: “And he had greaves of brass upon his legs, and a target of brass between his shoulders” (1Sa 17:6). The Spirit inventories Goliath’s armour piece by piece — helmet of brass, coat of mail weighing five thousand shekels, greaves of brass, target of brass, a spear staff like a weaver’s beam — and the whole catalogue is written to be undone. Israel counted the metal and trembled; David counted the LORD and came down to the brook. He would wear no armour at all, but took five smooth stones and a sling and met the giant with a better weapon than brass: “Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied” (1Sa 17:45). The greaves guarded the shins and left the forehead bare, and God guided the stone to the one place brass did not cover. So the boy declared the doctrine before he threw: “the LORD saveth not with sword and spear: for the battle is the LORD'S” (1Sa 17:47). The only armour that holds is the armour God Himself supplies, whose feet are shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace.
webster_summary: Armour for the shin, of brass or leather, worn from knee to ankle; in Scripture only of Goliath’s legs.
webster_full: GREAVES, armour for the legs; plates covering the shin from knee to ankle.
From the Old French greve, “the shin, the front of the leg.”
A KJV word occurring but once, of Goliath’s brass (1Sa 17:6).
Part of an inventory of armour written down that it might be undone.
They guarded the shins and left the forehead bare to the smooth stone.
scriptures: And he had greaves of brass upon his legs, and a target of brass between his shoulders.

Then said David to the Philistine, Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied.
And all this assembly shall know that the LORD saveth not with sword and spear: for the battle is the LORD'S, and he will give you into our hands.
Eph 6:15
And your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace;
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a piece of a giant’s armour; it recovers that the LORD saveth not with sword and spear, and that the only armour which holds is His.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a live temptation in the greaves, and every believer knows it. Goliath was brass from the crown of his head to his shins, and Israel counted the metal and fled — measuring the enemy’s equipment and forgetting the LORD of hosts. So the church still weighs the world’s armour: its numbers, its money, its platforms, its cleverness, and stands dismayed in the valley for forty days because the arithmetic is against her. But the Spirit wrote the inventory of that brass only to show how little it weighed against a boy with a sling. What terrifies faithless Israel is a detailed list of things God is about to break.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is stated by David before ever the stone flew: “the LORD saveth not with sword and spear: for the battle is the LORD'S.” Saul would have dressed the boy in his own armour, and David put it off, for borrowed brass had never been proved. The giant’s greaves guarded the shins and left the forehead bare, and the stone went where no metal was — God has no difficulty finding the gap in what men trust. The believer’s armour is not of his own forging: he takes the whole armour of God, his feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace, and goes out in a name that has never lost a battle.
roots_summary: The word means armour for the shin, worn from knee to ankle.
roots_lines: Greaves — Old French greve, “the shin.”
It denotes plates of brass or leather guarding the leg.
A KJV hapax, occurring only of Goliath (1Sa 17:6).
The giant’s brass was inventoried that it might be undone.
Against it stands the armour of God and the gospel of peace (Eph 6:15).
usage: Greaves of brass upon his legs: the Spirit lists the giant’s armour piece by piece, to break it.
David came in the name of the LORD of hosts, and brass availed the Philistine nothing.
The LORD saveth not with sword and spear — the battle is the LORD’S, and so is the victory.

etymology: Curious here in its older sense, from the Latin curiosus, “careful, done with pains and skill” — hence cunningly and skillfully wrought, not odd or strange. The curious girdle is the band of the ephod, woven of the same skilled work as the ephod itself.
biblical_def: The curious girdle is the woven band of the high priest’s ephod, and the adjective must be read in its old sense: curious means cunningly wrought, made with pains and skill, not odd. The LORD ordered it of one piece with the vesture: “And the curious girdle of the ephod, which is upon it, shall be of the same, according to the work thereof; even of gold, of blue, and purple” (Exo 28:8). Gold and blue and purple and scarlet and fine twined linen — the colours of the sanctuary itself, so that the man who bore Israel’s names went girded in the tabernacle’s own hues. Its office was to bind. By a lace of blue the breastplate was fastened to the rings of the ephod, “that it may be above the curious girdle of the ephod, and that the breastplate be not loosed from the ephod” (Exo 28:28): the girdle held the twelve tribes fast over the high priest’s heart, that no name should slip while he went in before the LORD. So Moses girded Aaron with it at his consecration (Exo 29:5; Lev 8:7), and thereafter no priest ministered ungirt. The type is not hidden. John saw the risen Christ in the midst of the candlesticks, “clothed with a garment down to the foot, and girt about the paps with a golden girdle” (Rev 1:13) — our great High Priest wearing the vesture of Aaron in glory, girded for service, with His people bound fast upon His heart and none of them loosed.
webster_summary: The skillfully wrought band of the high priest’s ephod, of one work with it, binding the breastplate fast above it.
webster_full: CURIOUS, in the old sense: wrought with care and skill; cunningly made. Not strange or odd.
From the Latin curiosus, “careful, done with pains.”
CURIOUS GIRDLE, the woven band of the ephod, of the same work as the ephod (Exo 28:8).
Of gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine twined linen — the colours of the sanctuary.
It bound the breastplate fast, that it be not loosed from the ephod (Exo 28:28).
scriptures: Exo 28:8
And the curious girdle of the ephod, which is upon it, shall be of the same, according to the work thereof; even of gold, of blue, and purple

And they shall bind the breastplate by the rings thereof unto the rings of the ephod with a lace of blue, that it may be above the curious girdle of the ephod, and that the breastplate be not loosed from the ephod.
Lev 8:7

And he put upon him the coat, and girded him with the girdle, and clothed him with the robe, and put the ephod upon him, and he girded him with the curious girdle of the ephod, and bound it unto him therewith.
Rev 1:13
And in the midst of the seven candlesticks one like unto the Son of man, clothed with a garment down to the foot, and girt about the paps with a golden girdle.
corruption_summary: A live misuse of a word: curious is read as odd, where the KJV means skillfully wrought — and the girdle itself recovers Christ our great High Priest, girded with His people bound fast upon His heart.
corruption_paragraphs: The misuse here is one of language, and it costs the reader a doctrine. Hearing curious, the modern ear supplies “odd, peculiar, strange” and imagines some quaint article of an obsolete religion. But the Authorized Version uses the word in its Latin sense — curiosus, careful, done with pains — and the curious girdle is the cunningly wrought band, the most skilled weaving in Israel, made by men whom God filled with His Spirit for that very work. There was nothing odd about it and nothing accidental: every thread of gold and blue and purple and scarlet was commanded from the mount, for God does not leave the furniture of His worship to the taste of the worshipper. To lose the word is to lose the care.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the girdle’s office, which is to bind and not to loose. The breastplate carried the names of the twelve tribes, and the lace of blue held it above the curious girdle “that the breastplate be not loosed from the ephod” — no tribe could slip from the high priest’s heart while he stood before God. Aaron’s girdle wore out and Aaron died; but John saw one like unto the Son of man, girt about the paps with a golden girdle, wearing the vesture of the priesthood in glory. The echo is deliberate: our great High Priest is girded for His service, and He bears His people’s names upon His heart where nothing can loose them.
roots_summary: The phrase means the skillfully wrought band of the ephod — curious in its old sense of cunningly made.
roots_lines: Curious — Latin curiosus, “careful, done with pains and skill.”
In the KJV it means cunningly wrought, never odd or strange.
Girdle — the band that girds and binds the vesture to the body.
The curious girdle was of one work with the ephod (Exo 28:8).
It held the breastplate fast, that it be not loosed (Exo 28:28).
usage: The curious girdle was cunningly wrought, not odd — the most skilled weaving in Israel.
It bound the breastplate above it, that the twelve names be not loosed from the ephod.

etymology: An older spelling of riband or ribbon, from the Middle English riban, probably from Old French ruban; hence a narrow band or strip of cloth. A KJV word occurring but once, of the blue thread bound upon the fringes of Israel’s garments.
biblical_def: A ribband is a narrow band or strip of cloth, and in Scripture it appears once, in a commandment about the hem of a garment. The LORD bade Israel “make them fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations, and that they put upon the fringe of the borders a ribband of blue” (Num 15:38). Blue was the colour of the sanctuary and of the heavens; a thread of it ran along the skirt of every Israelite, so that the commonest labourer carried a piece of the tabernacle on the hem of his coat. And God gave the reason plainly: “that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD, and do them; and that ye seek not after your own heart and your own eyes, after which ye use to go a whoring” (Num 15:39). There is the whole of it. The ribband was set against two rivals — your own heart and your own eyes — because those two are the fountains of every false worship man ever invented. The eye sees a thing it likes and the heart calls it holy, and so the calf is cast and the grove is planted. Against that, God gives a blue thread and a word: look, remember, do. The end is not sentiment but holiness: “That ye may remember, and do all my commandments, and be holy unto your God” (Num 15:40).
webster_summary: A narrow band or strip of cloth; in Numbers, the blue thread commanded upon the fringes of Israel’s garments as a memorial of the commandments.
webster_full: RIBBAND, a fillet; a narrow strip or band of cloth; an older spelling of riband or ribbon.
From Middle English riban, probably from Old French ruban.
A KJV word occurring but once, of the blue thread upon the fringe (Num 15:38).
Blue was the colour of the sanctuary, worn upon the hem of every Israelite.
Its end was memory and obedience, against the heart and the eyes (Num 15:39).
scriptures: Speak unto the children of Israel, and bid them that they make them fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations, and that they put upon the fringe of the borders a ribband of blue:

And it shall be unto you for a fringe, that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD, and do them; and that ye seek not after your own heart and your own eyes, after which ye use to go a whoring:
That ye may remember, and do all my commandments, and be holy unto your God.
Thou shalt make thee fringes upon the four quarters of thy vesture, wherewith thou coverest thyself.
corruption_summary: A live corruption: the ribband was hung against your own heart and your own eyes, and those two are precisely what the age has enthroned as the rule of life and worship.
corruption_paragraphs: Here is a corruption named by God Himself, and the age has adopted it as a creed. Follow your heart; trust your eyes; be true to yourself — this is the whole moral instruction of our time, printed on every wall and sung in every song. Numbers 15:39 answers it in one line: the ribband of blue was commanded “that ye seek not after your own heart and your own eyes, after which ye use to go a whoring.” God does not call the inner self a compass; He calls it a whoredom. The heart is deceitful above all things and desperately wicked (Jer 17:9), and the eye was the first thing Eve trusted when she saw that the tree was pleasant. A man who follows his heart is not finding himself; he is going after other gods with the hem of his garment bare.

The positive law is the regulative principle in a thread. God did not leave Israel to devise a memorial they found meaningful; He named the fringe, He named the colour, and He named the purpose — look, remember, do, and be holy unto your God. So it is in worship still: what God commands is required, and what He has not commanded is not ours to bring, however pleasing to the eye or dear to the heart. Every generation of the church is tempted to weave a hem of its own choosing and call it devotion; but the blue was heaven’s colour, chosen by heaven, and Israel’s part was to wear it and obey. Look upon the thread God gave, not the one you liked.
roots_summary: The word means a narrow band or strip of cloth — here the blue thread upon the fringe.
roots_lines: Ribband — an older spelling of riband, our ribbon.
From Middle English riban, probably from Old French ruban.
It denotes a narrow band or fillet of cloth.
A KJV hapax: the ribband of blue upon the fringe (Num 15:38).
Its end was memory, obedience, and holiness unto God (Num 15:40).
usage: A ribband of blue upon the fringe: the sanctuary’s colour worn on a labourer’s hem.
Look upon it and remember all the commandments of the LORD, and do them.
The thread was hung against your own heart and your own eyes — the two fountains of false worship.

etymology: Of uncertain origin, in Middle English pate, “the head, the crown or top of the head, the skull”; hence the scalp or crown. A KJV word occurring but once, at the end of the seventh psalm.
biblical_def: A pate is the crown or top of the head — the skull, the scalp, the very summit of a man. The word stands once in Scripture, and it stands at the end of a psalm about justice: “His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate” (Psa 7:16). David has been describing the wicked man at his work: he travails with iniquity, conceives mischief, brings forth falsehood; “He made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made” (Psa 7:15). The picture is of a man labouring hard at his own destruction — digging with sweat and care, and tumbling in. The pate is where the whole thing lands. Not on the innocent he hunted, not on some distant generation, but squarely on the top of his own head, in the exact measure he intended for another. This is not fate or irony; it is the government of God, who has ordained that sin be paid its wages. Solomon says the same: “Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him” (Pro 26:27), and Paul seals it: “God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap” (Gal 6:7). The pit-digger’s pate is the plainest doctrine of retribution in the Psalter, and the psalm ends not in gloating but in praise of the LORD’s righteousness.
webster_summary: The head; the crown or top of the head; the scalp. In Psalm 7 the place where the violent man’s own dealing lands.
webster_full: PATE, the head; the top of the head; the skull or scalp.
In Middle English pate, of uncertain origin, used commonly of the crown.
A KJV word occurring but once (Psa 7:16).
The violent man’s dealing comes down upon his own pate.
It figures the just retribution of God upon the sinner’s own head.
scriptures: Psa 7:16
His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate.
Psa 7:15
He made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made.
Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him.
Gal 6:7
Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but the old word for the crown of the head; it recovers the government of a God who is not mocked and pays every man his own measure.
corruption_paragraphs: The live misuse is to read this psalm as a proverb about consequences and nothing more — a piece of worldly wisdom about how bad choices catch up with people. That drains it. David is not observing a pattern; he is confessing a Judge. “God judgeth the righteous, and God is angry with the wicked every day” is the same psalm. The pit does not swallow the digger by accident of physics; the LORD, who tries the hearts and reins, brings the man’s mischief back upon his own pate in the very measure he had prepared for his neighbour. Take God out of the seventh psalm and you are left with a superstition; leave Him in, and you have justice.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is not mocked. A man may dig his pit in secret, roll his stone uphill in confidence, and reckon that the poor and the upright have no avenger — and every stroke of the spade is a stroke against his own skull. Whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap; the harvest is certain and the measure is exact. Yet mark how David ends: not with a laugh at the fallen but with worship — “I will praise the LORD according to his righteousness.” The saint takes no pleasure in the pate that is struck. He praises the God who governs, and he keeps his own hands from the spade.

The pate is not struck by accident: God is not mocked, and every man reaps what he sows.

etymology: From the Middle English pappe, of imitative origin (the infant’s sound at the breast); hence the breast, the teat that gives suck. Commonly in the plural, paps, in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: A pap is the breast that gives suck — the plain old English word the Authorized Version uses where a modern version would say breast. Its great occurrence is a beatitude interrupted. As Christ was speaking, “a certain woman of the company lifted up her voice, and said unto him, Blessed is the womb that bare thee, and the paps which thou hast sucked” (Luk 11:27). It was warmly meant. And our Lord would not have it: “Yea rather, blessed are they that hear the word of God, and keep it” (Luk 11:28). He did not deny that Mary was blessed; He moved the blessing. The honour does not rest where a woman thought to put it — on the womb and the breast, on flesh and kinship — but upon hearing and keeping the word, which is open to the poorest hearer in the crowd. The word turns again in the Olivet warning, where the paps that never gave suck are called blessed in a day of wrath (Luk 23:29), and again in Ezekiel, where Israel’s harlotry is charged in the coarse language of the body (Eze 23:21) — for Scripture is not delicate about sin. And it rises to glory in the Revelation: John saw one like unto the Son of man “girt about the paps with a golden girdle” (Rev 1:13), the risen Christ wearing the high-priestly vesture in the midst of the candlesticks.
webster_summary: The breast; the teat that gives suck. In Luke, the paps a woman called blessed — a blessing Christ moved to the hearers of the word.
webster_full: PAP, a nipple; a teat; the breast that gives suck. Chiefly in the plural, paps.
From Middle English pappe, of imitative origin.
“Blessed is the womb that bare thee, and the paps which thou hast sucked” (Luk 11:27).
Christ answered, “Yea rather, blessed are they that hear the word of God, and keep it.”
The risen Christ is girt about the paps with a golden girdle (Rev 1:13).
scriptures: And it came to pass, as he spake these things, a certain woman of the company lifted up her voice, and said unto him, Blessed is the womb that bare thee, and the paps which thou hast sucked.
But he said, Yea rather, blessed are they that hear the word of God, and keep it.
Rev 1:13
And in the midst of the seven candlesticks one like unto the Son of man, clothed with a garment down to the foot, and girt about the paps with a golden girdle.
Thus thou calledst to remembrance the lewdness of thy youth, in bruising thy teats by the Egyptians for the paps of thy youth.
corruption_summary: A live corruption: Marian devotion builds upon the very blessing Christ refused, for He took the beatitude off His mother’s womb and paps and laid it upon the hearers of the word.
corruption_paragraphs: This is one of the few places where our Lord Himself forecloses a corruption before it is born. A woman blessed the womb that bare Him and the paps which He had sucked, and Christ answered, “Yea rather, blessed are they that hear the word of God, and keep it.” Rome has spent fifteen centuries building on the sentence He set aside. The cult of the Virgin — the rosary, the Hail Mary, the titles of Mediatrix and Queen of Heaven, the dogmas of the immaculate conception and the bodily assumption, the prayers addressed to her and the merit sought through her — is precisely the blessing this woman offered, magnified and made into worship. Mary was blessed among women, and every generation calls her blessed; but she called God her Saviour, and she needed one. There is one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, and He accepts no colleague.

Mark how gently and how firmly Christ moves the honour. He does not scold the woman or deny His mother; He says yea rather — there is a better blessedness, and it is not reserved to a womb. Kinship to Christ after the flesh saves no one; the same Gospel records that His brethren did not believe on Him. What is open to every soul in that crowd, and to every reader of this page, is to hear the word of God and keep it. That is where He put the beatitude, and no church has authority to move it back. To pray to Mary is to seek a mediator Christ never appointed; to hear and keep His word is to be counted His mother and His brother and His sister indeed.

etymology: From the Old English clūt, “a patch, a piece of cloth or metal, a rag”; hence a rag, a patch, and as a verb clouted, patched or mended. Not the modern sense of a blow or of influence.
biblical_def: A clout is a rag or a patch — a scrap of worn cloth, the meanest thing in a house. The KJV knows nothing of our clout meaning a blow or a man’s influence; a clout is what you would throw away. The word’s great hour is in a dungeon. Jeremiah had been let down with cords into the mire of the pit to die, and Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, a foreigner and a eunuch in the king’s house, obtained leave to draw him out: “Ebedmelech took the men with him, and went into the house of the king under the treasury, and took thence old cast clouts and old rotten rags, and let them down by cords into the dungeon to Jeremiah” (Jer 38:11). Then he called down the tenderest instruction in the book: “Put now these old cast clouts and rotten rags under thine armholes under the cords” (Jer 38:12) — lest the ropes cut the starved prophet’s arms as they hauled him up. A heathen’s kindness thought of the man’s bruises when all Judah wanted him dead, and God did not forget it. The word appears once more, in the Gibeonites’ fraud: they came with “old shoes and clouted upon their feet, and old garments upon them” (Jos 9:5), patched and travel-worn, to counterfeit a long journey. So the clout runs two ways — the rags of a kindness God remembered, and the rags of a lie Israel believed because they asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD.
webster_summary: A rag or patch; a piece of worn cloth. In Jeremiah, the old cast clouts let down to lift the prophet out of the dungeon.
webster_full: CLOUT, a patch; a rag; a piece of cloth used to mend.
From the Saxon clūt, “a patch, a piece of cloth”; not the modern blow or influence.
As a participle, clouted: patched, mended (Jos 9:5).
Old cast clouts and rotten rags drew Jeremiah from the mire (Jer 38:11).
Ebedmelech bade him put them under his armholes, lest the cords cut him (Jer 38:12).
scriptures: So Ebedmelech took the men with him, and went into the house of the king under the treasury, and took thence old cast clouts and old rotten rags, and let them down by cords into the dungeon to Jeremiah.
And Ebedmelech the Ethiopian said unto Jeremiah, Put now these old cast clouts and rotten rags under thine armholes under the cords. And Jeremiah did so.
So they drew up Jeremiah with cords, and took him up out of the dungeon: and Jeremiah remained in the court of the prison.
Jos 9:5
And old shoes and clouted upon their feet, and old garments upon them; and all the bread of their provision was dry and mouldy.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but the old word for a rag; it recovers a heathen’s kindness to a prophet, and the warning that patched rags can carry a lie as well as a mercy.
corruption_paragraphs: The live misuse is the word itself, and it hides a story. Modern English has emptied clout into a blow or into influence — who has clout, who wields it — so that a reader coming to Jeremiah 38 sees nothing but an obscure archaism and passes over one of the gentlest deeds in the Old Testament. Recover the plain sense and the scene opens: a starved prophet standing to the armpits in mire, and an Ethiopian rummaging under the king’s treasury for rags soft enough to pad the ropes. The world’s clout is power; the Bible’s clout is a rag in the hand of a kind man. It is worth noticing which one God wrote down.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the worth of small kindness and the danger of unexamined rags. Ebedmelech was a foreigner and a servant, with no standing in Judah and nothing to gain; the princes had cast Jeremiah in to die and the king had let them. He fetched old cast clouts, thought of the man’s bruised armholes, and drew him up — and the LORD sent word to that Ethiopian by name: “I will surely deliver thee… because thou hast put thy trust in me.” Yet the Gibeonites came in clouted shoes and old garments, and Israel believed the rags because they asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD. Kindness is remembered; appearances are not to be trusted. Both lessons hang on a scrap of cloth.

etymology: From the Old French dameisele, a diminutive of dame (“lady”), from the Latin domina, “mistress of a house”; hence a young unmarried woman, a maiden, a girl.
biblical_def: A damsel is a young unmarried woman — a maiden, a girl not yet given to a husband. The word is the Authorized Version’s ordinary term, and it is never a slight; its root is domina, a lady. Abraham’s servant prayed by the well that the LORD would appoint the damsel who should water his camels, and “the damsel was very fair to look upon, a virgin, neither had any man known her” (Gen 24:16) — Scripture notices her chastity as a thing worth recording, and the marriage of Isaac turned upon it. The word’s highest hour is at a deathbed in Capernaum. The mourners laughed Christ to scorn when He said the damsel was not dead but sleeping; He put them all out, took her by the hand, and said, “Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise” (Mar 5:41). “And straightway the damsel arose, and walked” (Mar 5:42) — twelve years old, and raised by a word, for the Lord of life speaks to the dead as a father wakes a child in the morning. Elsewhere a damsel named Rhoda hears Peter at the gate and, for gladness, forgets to open it (Act 12:13) — and the praying church calls her mad, though she was the only one who believed the prayer answered. From Rebekah at the well to Jairus’s daughter on her bed, the damsels of Scripture are named, guarded by God’s law, and dealt with tenderly by Christ.
webster_summary: A young unmarried woman; a maiden; a girl. From the Latin domina, a lady — never a term of slight.
webster_full: DAMSEL, a young woman or girl; a maiden not yet married.
From Old French dameisele, a diminutive of dame, from Latin domina, “lady.”
Rebekah was a damsel very fair to look upon, a virgin (Gen 24:16).
Christ raised the damsel of Jairus with a word: “Damsel, I say unto thee, arise” (Mar 5:41).
Rhoda, a damsel of the praying church, heard Peter at the gate (Act 12:13).
scriptures: And the damsel was very fair to look upon, a virgin, neither had any man known her: and she went down to the well, and filled her pitcher, and came up.
Mar 5:41
And he took the damsel by the hand, and said unto her, Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise.
Mar 5:42
And straightway the damsel arose, and walked; for she was of the age of twelve years. And they were astonished with a great astonishment.
And as Peter knocked at the door of the gate, a damsel came to hearken, named Rhoda.
corruption_summary: A live corruption: the age has made the maiden a joke and her purity a punchline, where God’s law guarded her, His Word named her, and Christ took her by the hand.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is a mockery. Damsel survives in modern speech only in a sneer — the damsel in distress, the helpless maiden who wants rescuing — and the sneer is aimed past the word at the thing itself: at maidenhood, at chastity before marriage, at a young woman under her father’s roof and God’s law. The age teaches a girl that her virginity is an embarrassment to be disposed of early and her father’s protection an insult to be escaped. Scripture speaks otherwise and without apology. It records of Rebekah that she was a virgin, neither had any man known her, and it does so because the fact is honourable. Deuteronomy 22 hedges the betrothed damsel about with a law that puts her violator to death and, when she is forced in the field where none could save her, says plainly “unto the damsel thou shalt do nothing.” That is not contempt for women; that is a God who counts them worth defending with the sword of the magistrate.

And see how the Lord Himself handles a damsel. The house was full of noise and professional mourners, and He put them all out; He would not have a twelve-year-old girl raised as a spectacle. He took her by the hand — touching the dead, which no priest would do — and spoke to her in her mother’s Aramaic, Talitha cumi, the homeliest words a child could wake to. Then He commanded that something be given her to eat, because she would be hungry. There is the measure of Christ’s regard for the daughters of men: sovereign power over death, exercised with the tenderness of a father at a bedside. An age that jeers at the damsel has never seen her as her Maker sees her, nor watched her Saviour take her by the hand.
